Step 48 — Robust Cross-Validation Benchmark¶
The previous experiments used a single stratified validation split. Since we have now used that validation set repeatedly for model selection, its score is no longer an unbiased estimate of final generalization performance.


We will now evaluate the selected LightGBM configuration using Stratified K-Fold cross-validation.


Why Stratified K-Fold?


    

  • The target has three damage grades with substantial class imbalance.
    • 

  • Stratification preserves approximately the same class proportions in every fold.
    • 

  • Multiple validation folds provide a more stable estimate than a single split.
    • 

  • We will report the Micro-F1 score for every fold as well as the mean and standard deviation.
    • 



For this benchmark we will use the best configuration found so far rather than performing another expensive hyperparameter search.


Important:
Micro-F1 is equal to accuracy for this single-label multiclass problem, so both metrics will have the same value.












In [118]:






from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, accuracy_score
import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import time


# Best configuration found during our previous experiments
cv_model_params = {
    "objective": "multiclass",
    "num_class": 3,
    "n_estimators": 1200,
    "learning_rate": 0.03,
    "num_leaves": 15,
    "min_child_samples": 200,
    "colsample_bytree": 0.8,
    "subsample": 0.8,
    "subsample_freq": 1,
    "max_depth": -1,
    "random_state": RANDOM_STATE,
    "n_jobs": -1,
    "force_col_wise": True
}


# Stratified 5-fold cross-validation
skf = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)


cv_results = []

start_time = time.time()

for fold, (train_idx, valid_idx) in enumerate(
    skf.split(X, y),
    start=1
):
    print(f"\n{'=' * 60}")
    print(f"Fold {fold}/5")
    print(f"{'=' * 60}")

    X_fold_train = X.iloc[train_idx].copy()
    X_fold_valid = X.iloc[valid_idx].copy()

    y_fold_train = y.iloc[train_idx]
    y_fold_valid = y.iloc[valid_idx]

    # Convert categorical columns to pandas category dtype
    for col in LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS:
        X_fold_train[col] = X_fold_train[col].astype("category")
        X_fold_valid[col] = X_fold_valid[col].astype("category")

    model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(**cv_model_params)

    model.fit(
        X_fold_train,
        y_fold_train,
        categorical_feature=LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS
    )

    y_fold_pred = model.predict(X_fold_valid)

    accuracy = accuracy_score(
        y_fold_valid,
        y_fold_pred
    )

    micro_f1 = f1_score(
        y_fold_valid,
        y_fold_pred,
        average="micro"
    )

    macro_f1 = f1_score(
        y_fold_valid,
        y_fold_pred,
        average="macro"
    )

    weighted_f1 = f1_score(
        y_fold_valid,
        y_fold_pred,
        average="weighted"
    )

    cv_results.append({
        "fold": fold,
        "accuracy": accuracy,
        "micro_f1": micro_f1,
        "macro_f1": macro_f1,
        "weighted_f1": weighted_f1
    })

    print(f"Accuracy:    {accuracy:.4f}")
    print(f"Micro-F1:    {micro_f1:.4f}")
    print(f"Macro-F1:    {macro_f1:.4f}")
    print(f"Weighted-F1: {weighted_f1:.4f}")


cv_results_df = pd.DataFrame(cv_results)

elapsed_minutes = (time.time() - start_time) / 60

print(f"\nTotal CV time: {elapsed_minutes:.2f} minutes")

display(cv_results_df)


print("\nCross-validation summary:")
print(
    f"Mean Micro-F1: {cv_results_df['micro_f1'].mean():.4f}"
)
print(
    f"Std Micro-F1:  {cv_results_df['micro_f1'].std():.4f}"
)
print(
    f"Min Micro-F1:  {cv_results_df['micro_f1'].min():.4f}"
)
print(
    f"Max Micro-F1:  {cv_results_df['micro_f1'].max():.4f}"
)

Step 49 — Cross-Validation Error Analysis¶
The target damage_grade is ordinal:


1 = low damage
2 = medium damage
3 = severe damage


Therefore, not all classification errors are equally informative.


For example:


    

  • predicting Grade 2 for a true Grade 1 is an adjacent error;
    • 

  • predicting Grade 3 for a true Grade 1 is a two-level error.
    • 



We will examine the cross-validation predictions to determine:


    

  1. Which damage grades are hardest to predict.
    2. 

  2. Which grade pairs are most commonly confused.
    3. 

  3. Whether errors are predominantly adjacent ordinal errors.
    4. 

  4. Whether the model systematically underpredicts or overpredicts damage severity.
    5. 



This will guide the next modeling decision.












In [119]:






from sklearn.metrics import (
    confusion_matrix,
    classification_report,
    f1_score,
    accuracy_score
)

# Store out-of-fold predictions
oof_predictions = np.empty(len(y), dtype=int)

for fold, (train_idx, valid_idx) in enumerate(
    skf.split(X, y),
    start=1
):
    X_fold_train = X.iloc[train_idx].copy()
    X_fold_valid = X.iloc[valid_idx].copy()

    y_fold_train = y.iloc[train_idx]
    y_fold_valid = y.iloc[valid_idx]

    for col in LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS:
        X_fold_train[col] = X_fold_train[col].astype("category")
        X_fold_valid[col] = X_fold_valid[col].astype("category")

    model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(**cv_model_params)

    model.fit(
        X_fold_train,
        y_fold_train,
        categorical_feature=LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS
    )

    oof_predictions[valid_idx] = model.predict(
        X_fold_valid
    ).astype(int)


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Overall metrics
# ---------------------------------------------------------

print("OOF Accuracy:", accuracy_score(y, oof_predictions))
print(
    "OOF Micro-F1:",
    f1_score(y, oof_predictions, average="micro")
)
print(
    "OOF Macro-F1:",
    f1_score(y, oof_predictions, average="macro")
)
print(
    "OOF Weighted-F1:",
    f1_score(y, oof_predictions, average="weighted")
)


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Confusion matrix
# ---------------------------------------------------------

cm = confusion_matrix(
    y,
    oof_predictions,
    labels=[1, 2, 3]
)

cm_df = pd.DataFrame(
    cm,
    index=["True 1", "True 2", "True 3"],
    columns=["Pred 1", "Pred 2", "Pred 3"]
)

display(cm_df)


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Per-class classification report
# ---------------------------------------------------------

report = classification_report(
    y,
    oof_predictions,
    labels=[1, 2, 3],
    target_names=[
        "Grade 1",
        "Grade 2",
        "Grade 3"
    ],
    output_dict=True
)

report_df = pd.DataFrame(report).T

display(
    report_df.loc[
        ["Grade 1", "Grade 2", "Grade 3"],
        ["precision", "recall", "f1-score", "support"]
    ]
)


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Ordinal error analysis
# ---------------------------------------------------------

y_array = y.to_numpy()

error_mask = y_array != oof_predictions

ordinal_distance = np.abs(
    y_array - oof_predictions
)

adjacent_errors = np.sum(
    error_mask & (ordinal_distance == 1)
)

two_level_errors = np.sum(
    error_mask & (ordinal_distance == 2)
)

total_errors = np.sum(error_mask)

print(f"Total errors:              {total_errors:,}")
print(f"Adjacent errors:           {adjacent_errors:,}")
print(f"Two-level errors:          {two_level_errors:,}")

if total_errors > 0:
    print(
        f"Adjacent error percentage: "
        f"{adjacent_errors / total_errors:.2%}"
    )
    print(
        f"Two-level error percentage: "
        f"{two_level_errors / total_errors:.2%}"
    )


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Error rate by true grade
# ---------------------------------------------------------

error_by_grade = []

for grade in [1, 2, 3]:
    mask = y_array == grade

    total = mask.sum()
    errors = np.sum(
        mask & (oof_predictions != grade)
    )

    error_by_grade.append({
        "true_grade": grade,
        "n_samples": total,
        "n_errors": errors,
        "error_rate": errors / total
    })

error_by_grade_df = pd.DataFrame(error_by_grade)

display(error_by_grade_df)

Step 51 — XGBoost Multiclass Baseline¶
We now move from LightGBM to XGBoost.


The purpose of this experiment is to establish a comparable XGBoost benchmark using the same training/validation framework.


We will:


    

  • use the original structural and geographic features;
    • 

  • one-hot encode the low-cardinality categorical variables;
    • 

  • retain the geographic IDs as numeric features;
    • 

  • use the same Stratified K-Fold strategy;
    • 

  • evaluate using Micro-F1;
    • 

  • report Macro-F1 as a secondary metric.
    • 



We will initially avoid:


    

  • target encoding;
    • 

  • additional feature engineering;
    • 

  • another expensive grid search.
    • 



This gives us a clean comparison between LightGBM and XGBoost.


Reference:
LightGBM 5-fold CV Micro-F1 = approximately 0.7487 ± 0.0012.












In [131]:






from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.metrics import (
    f1_score,
    accuracy_score,
    classification_report
)
from xgboost import XGBClassifier

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import time


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Features
# ---------------------------------------------------------

X_xgb = X.copy()
y_xgb = y.copy()



# Categorical columns
XGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS = CATEGORICAL_COLS.copy()


# Numeric columns
XGB_NUMERIC_COLS = [
    col for col in X_xgb.columns
    if col not in XGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS
]


print("XGBoost numeric columns:", len(XGB_NUMERIC_COLS))
print("XGBoost categorical columns:", len(XGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS))
print("Total input columns:", X_xgb.shape[1])


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# One-hot encoding
# ---------------------------------------------------------

xgb_preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        (
            "categorical",
            OneHotEncoder(
                handle_unknown="ignore",
                sparse_output=True
            ),
            XGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS
        ),
        (
            "numeric",
            "passthrough",
            XGB_NUMERIC_COLS
        )
    ]
)


X_xgb_encoded = xgb_preprocessor.fit_transform(X_xgb)


print("\nEncoded feature matrix shape:")
print(X_xgb_encoded.shape)



















XGBoost numeric columns: 30
XGBoost categorical columns: 8
Total input columns: 38

Encoded feature matrix shape:
(260601, 68)



















Step 51B — Train the XGBoost Baseline¶
The baseline uses the histogram-based tree algorithm (tree_method="hist") because the dataset contains approximately 260K training observations.


We use multiclass soft probabilities internally and convert them into the predicted damage grade.


The first objective is not to optimize every XGBoost parameter. It is to establish a reliable baseline that can be compared against LightGBM.












In [132]:






# ---------------------------------------------------------
# XGBoost baseline parameters
# ---------------------------------------------------------

xgb_params = {
    "objective": "multi:softprob",
    "num_class": 3,

    "n_estimators": 800,
    "learning_rate": 0.05,

    "max_depth": 6,
    "min_child_weight": 1,

    "subsample": 0.8,
    "colsample_bytree": 0.8,

    "gamma": 0,

    "reg_alpha": 0,
    "reg_lambda": 1,

    "tree_method": "hist",

    "eval_metric": "mlogloss",

    "random_state": RANDOM_STATE,
    "n_jobs": -1
}


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Stratified 5-fold CV
# ---------------------------------------------------------

skf_xgb = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)


xgb_cv_results = []

start_time = time.time()


for fold, (train_idx, valid_idx) in enumerate(
    skf_xgb.split(X_xgb_encoded, y_xgb),
    start=1
):

    print(f"\n{'=' * 60}")
    print(f"XGBoost Fold {fold}/5")
    print(f"{'=' * 60}")

    X_fold_train = X_xgb_encoded[train_idx]
    X_fold_valid = X_xgb_encoded[valid_idx]

    y_fold_train = y_xgb.iloc[train_idx]
    y_fold_valid = y_xgb.iloc[valid_idx]

    model = XGBClassifier(**xgb_params)

    model.fit(
        X_fold_train,
        y_fold_train - 1
    )

    y_pred = model.predict(
        X_fold_valid
    ).astype(int) + 1

    accuracy = accuracy_score(
        y_fold_valid,
        y_pred
    )

    micro_f1 = f1_score(
        y_fold_valid,
        y_pred,
        average="micro"
    )

    macro_f1 = f1_score(
        y_fold_valid,
        y_pred,
        average="macro"
    )

    weighted_f1 = f1_score(
        y_fold_valid,
        y_pred,
        average="weighted"
    )

    xgb_cv_results.append({
        "fold": fold,
        "accuracy": accuracy,
        "micro_f1": micro_f1,
        "macro_f1": macro_f1,
        "weighted_f1": weighted_f1
    })

    print(f"Accuracy:    {accuracy:.4f}")
    print(f"Micro-F1:    {micro_f1:.4f}")
    print(f"Macro-F1:    {macro_f1:.4f}")
    print(f"Weighted-F1: {weighted_f1:.4f}")


xgb_cv_results_df = pd.DataFrame(
    xgb_cv_results
)


elapsed_minutes = (
    time.time() - start_time
) / 60


print(f"\nTotal XGBoost CV time: {elapsed_minutes:.2f} minutes")

display(xgb_cv_results_df)


print("\nXGBoost Cross-validation summary:")

print(
    f"Mean Micro-F1: "
    f"{xgb_cv_results_df['micro_f1'].mean():.4f}"
)

print(
    f"Std Micro-F1:  "
    f"{xgb_cv_results_df['micro_f1'].std():.4f}"
)

print(
    f"Min Micro-F1:  "
    f"{xgb_cv_results_df['micro_f1'].min():.4f}"
)

print(

Step 52 — SHAP Model Explainability¶
We have now compared the main candidate models:


    

  • Logistic Regression
    • 

  • Random Forest
    • 

  • XGBoost
    • 

  • LightGBM
    • 



LightGBM is the strongest model based on cross-validation Micro-F1.


We will therefore use SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to interpret the selected LightGBM model.


The analysis will focus on:


    

  1. Global feature importance.
    2. 

  2. Which features most strongly influence severe damage (Grade 3).
    3. 

  3. The direction of important feature effects where possible.
    4. 

  4. Whether geographic variables dominate the model.
    5. 

  5. Whether structural characteristics such as foundation type,
superstructure and building age remain important after geographic
information is considered.
    6. 



SHAP is being used for interpretation rather than feature selection.
A feature with high SHAP importance is not automatically a feature
that should be removed or retained without considering model
performance and domain meaning.

# Train the LGB model for SHAP

import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Use the validated 41-feature geographic model
# ---------------------------------------------------------

X_shap_train = X_train_geo.copy()
X_shap_valid = X_valid_geo.copy()

y_shap_train = y_train.copy()
y_shap_valid = y_valid.copy()


print("Training shape:", X_shap_train.shape)
print("Validation shape:", X_shap_valid.shape)


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Identify categorical columns actually present
# ---------------------------------------------------------

LGBM_CATEGORICAL_COLS = [
    col for col in CATEGORICAL_COLS
    if col in X_shap_train.columns
]

print("\nCategorical columns:")
print(LGBM_CATEGORICAL_COLS)


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Make categorical columns explicit
# ---------------------------------------------------------

for col in LGBM_CATEGORICAL_COLS:
    X_shap_train[col] = X_shap_train[col].astype("category")
    X_shap_valid[col] = X_shap_valid[col].astype("category")

    # Make validation categories identical to training categories
    X_shap_valid[col] = X_shap_valid[col].cat.set_categories(
        X_shap_train[col].cat.categories
    )


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# LightGBM model
#
# Parameters based on our previous experiments.
# num_leaves = 15
# min_child_samples = 200
# subsample = 0.8
# colsample_bytree = 0.8
# ---------------------------------------------------------

shap_lgbm = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
    objective="multiclass",
    num_class=3,

    n_estimators=1000,
    learning_rate=0.05,

    num_leaves=15,
    min_child_samples=200,

    subsample=0.8,
    colsample_bytree=0.8,

    reg_alpha=0,
    reg_lambda=0,

    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=-1,

    verbosity=-1
)


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Train with early stopping
# ---------------------------------------------------------

shap_lgbm.fit(
    X_shap_train,
    y_shap_train,

    categorical_feature=LGBM_CATEGORICAL_COLS,

    eval_set=[
        (X_shap_valid, y_shap_valid)
    ],

    callbacks=[
        lgb.early_stopping(
            stopping_rounds=100,
            verbose=False
        )
    ]
)


print("\nBest iteration:", shap_lgbm.best_iteration_)

X_shap_train = X_train.copy()
X_shap_valid = X_valid.copy()

y_shap_train = y_train.copy()
y_shap_valid = y_valid.copy()


# Convert categorical columns
for col in CATEGORICAL_COLS:
    X_shap_train[col] = X_shap_train[col].astype("category")
    X_shap_valid[col] = X_shap_valid[col].astype("category")

    # Ensure identical category definitions
    X_shap_valid[col] = X_shap_valid[col].cat.set_categories(
        X_shap_train[col].cat.categories
    )


# All categorical features, including geographic IDs
LGBM_SHAP_CATEGORICAL_COLS = [
    col for col in GEO_COLS + CATEGORICAL_COLS
    if col in X_shap_train.columns
]


shap_lgbm = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
    objective="multiclass",
    num_class=3,

    n_estimators=1200,
    learning_rate=0.03,

    num_leaves=15,
    min_child_samples=200,

    colsample_bytree=0.8,

    # Explicitly activate row subsampling
    subsample=0.8,
    subsample_freq=1,

    max_depth=-1,

    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=-1,

    force_col_wise=True,
    verbosity=-1
)


shap_lgbm.fit(
    X_shap_train,
    y_shap_train,

    categorical_feature=LGBM_SHAP_CATEGORICAL_COLS,

    eval_set=[
        (X_shap_valid, y_shap_valid)
    ],

    callbacks=[
        lgb.early_stopping(
            stopping_rounds=100,
            verbose=False
        )
    ]
)


print("Best iteration:", shap_lgbm.best_iteration_)

SHAP analysis sample¶
SHAP explanations can be computationally expensive, especially for a multiclass
tree model. To keep the analysis practical while retaining a representative
sample, we use 5,000 randomly selected validation observations.


The validation set is used only for explanation here; the model itself was trained
on the training split.












In [139]:






# ---------------------------------------------------------
# SHAP analysis sample
# ---------------------------------------------------------

SHAP_SAMPLE_SIZE = 5000

X_shap_sample = X_shap_valid.sample(
    n=min(SHAP_SAMPLE_SIZE, len(X_shap_valid)),
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)

print("SHAP sample shape:", X_shap_sample.shape)



















SHAP sample shape: (5000, 38)



















Calculate SHAP values¶
We use TreeExplainer because LightGBM is a tree-based model.


For each building and each feature, the SHAP value represents that feature's
contribution to the model's output relative to the model's baseline prediction.


Since damage grade is multiclass, SHAP values are calculated separately for
grades 1, 2, and 3.












In [140]:






import shap
import numpy as np

# Create TreeExplainer for the trained LightGBM model
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(shap_lgbm)

# Calculate SHAP values
shap_values = explainer.shap_values(X_shap_sample)

print("SHAP output type:", type(shap_values))

if isinstance(shap_values, list):
    print("Number of class outputs:", len(shap_values))
    for i, values in enumerate(shap_values):
        print(f"Class {i + 1} SHAP shape:", values.shape)
else:
    print("SHAP array shape:", np.asarray(shap_values).shape)



















SHAP output type: <class 'numpy.ndarray'>
SHAP array shape: (5000, 38, 3)



















Global SHAP feature importance¶
Mean absolute SHAP value measures how strongly each feature influences the
model's predictions, regardless of whether the feature pushes the prediction
toward a higher or lower damage grade.


For the multiclass model, we aggregate the absolute SHAP values across all
three damage-grade outputs.


This measures model reliance, not causal importance.


Which building features does the model rely on most overall?












In [141]:






# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Global SHAP feature importance
# ---------------------------------------------------------

# SHAP shape:
# (n_samples, n_features, n_classes)

global_shap_importance = np.mean(
    np.abs(shap_values),
    axis=(0, 2)
)

global_shap_importance_df = (
    pd.DataFrame({
        "feature": X_shap_sample.columns,
        "mean_abs_shap": global_shap_importance
    })
    .sort_values("mean_abs_shap", ascending=False)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

global_shap_importance_df["rank"] = (
    np.arange(1, len(global_shap_importance_df) + 1)
)

global_shap_importance_df = global_shap_importance_df[
    ["rank", "feature", "mean_abs_shap"]
]

SHAP analysis for damage grade 3¶

Positive SHAP values indicate that a feature pushes the model toward the

Mean absolute SHAP values measure the strength of the contribution, while
the signed values allow us to investigate its direction.

Direction of feature effects on damage grade 3¶
Mean absolute SHAP values tell us which features matter most, but not the
direction of their effect.


Here we examine signed SHAP values for the grade-3 output.


Positive SHAP values indicate that a feature pushes a prediction toward
near-total destruction (grade 3), while negative values push it away from
grade 3.


For categorical variables, the relationship must be interpreted by category
rather than treating the category codes as ordered numerical values.












In [146]:

    print(
        temp.groupby("feature_value")["shap_value"]
        .agg(["mean", "median", "count"])

Categorical feature effects on grade 3¶
For categorical features, we calculate the mean signed Grade-3 SHAP value
within each category.


This allows us to identify which observed categories tend to push the model
toward grade 3 and which tend to push it away.


These are model associations rather than causal effects.












In [148]:






# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Categorical feature -> Grade 3 SHAP direction
# ---------------------------------------------------------

categorical_features_for_shap = [
    col for col in CATEGORICAL_COLS
    if col in X_shap_sample.columns
]

categorical_shap_results = {}

for feature in categorical_features_for_shap:

    feature_idx = X_shap_sample.columns.get_loc(feature)

    temp = pd.DataFrame({
        "category": X_shap_sample[feature].astype(str).to_numpy(),
        "grade3_shap": shap_values_grade3[:, feature_idx]
    })

    summary = (
        temp
        .groupby("category")["grade3_shap"]
        .agg(
            mean_shap="mean",
            median_shap="median",
            mean_abs_shap=lambda x: np.mean(np.abs(x)),
            count="count"
        )
        .sort_values("mean_shap", ascending=False)
    )

    categorical_shap_results[feature] = summary

    print(f"\n{'=' * 80}")
    print(f"{feature}")
    print(f"{'=' * 80}")

    display(summary)

Grade 3 SHAP summary plot¶
The SHAP beeswarm plot combines feature importance and direction.


Features are ordered by mean absolute SHAP value. Each point represents one
building in the SHAP sample.


The horizontal position represents the signed SHAP contribution:


    

  • positive values push the model toward damage grade 3
    • 

  • negative values push the model away from damage grade 3
    • 



For numerical features, point position also shows how the feature value
relates to the model contribution.

Step 53 — Train the final LightGBM model¶
The final model uses the original 38 features.


Feature-engineering experiments involving:


    

  • geographic target encoding,
    • 

  • geographic hierarchy combinations,
    • 

  • structural interaction features,
    • 

  • and age bands
    • 



did not improve validation performance, so they are excluded.


The final model is trained using all available labelled training observations
before generating predictions for the test dataset.












In [150]:






# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Final LightGBM model
# ---------------------------------------------------------

X_final = X.copy()
X_test_final = X_test.copy()

# Convert categorical features to pandas category
for col in CATEGORICAL_COLS:
    X_final[col] = X_final[col].astype("category")
    X_test_final[col] = X_test_final[col].astype("category")

    # Ensure train/test use identical category definitions
    X_test_final[col] = X_test_final[col].cat.set_categories(
        X_final[col].cat.categories
    )

FINAL_LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS = [
    col for col in GEO_COLS + CATEGORICAL_COLS
    if col in X_final.columns
]

final_lgbm = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
    objective="multiclass",
    num_class=3,

    n_estimators=870,
    learning_rate=0.03,

    num_leaves=15,
    min_child_samples=200,

    colsample_bytree=0.8,

    subsample=0.8,
    subsample_freq=1,

    max_depth=-1,

    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=-1,

    force_col_wise=True,
    verbosity=-1
)

final_lgbm.fit(
    X_final,
    y,

    categorical_feature=FINAL_LGB_CATEGORICAL_COLS
)

print("Final model trained.")
print("Number of features:", X_final.shape[1])
print("Number of training rows:", X_final.shape[0])

Feature Engineering¶
Eight new features derived from the raw columns, chosen from patterns surfaced during EDA
(Sections 3, 6, 8, 9). All are deterministic functions of the raw features only -- no target
information is used, so they can be computed identically and independently on train and test
with no leakage risk.












In [71]:






def engineer_features(df):
    df = df.copy()

    # age is retained raw (Data Retention Decision) -- flag the 995 sentinel explicitly
    # so the model can separate it from genuinely old buildings.
    df["age_is_placeholder"] = (df["age"] == 995).astype(int)

    # Coarse life-stage buckets -- captures non-linear age thresholds a single continuous
    # term can't, and gives age==995 its own category ("unknown") instead of forcing it
    # into "very_old" alongside genuinely long-lived buildings. The max age in this dataset
    # is exactly 995 (EDA Section 6), so the (994, inf) bin only ever catches the sentinel.
    df["age_bucket"] = pd.cut(
        df["age"], bins=[-1, 5, 15, 30, 994, 10_000],
        labels=["new", "moderate", "old", "very_old", "unknown"],
    ).astype(str)

    # Older AND taller compounds risk; both are individually weak predictors (Section 9).
    df["age_x_floors"] = df["age"] * df["count_floors_pre_eq"]

    # Slenderness proxy -- height_percentage correlates +0.05 with damage, area_percentage
    # correlates -0.13 (Section 9); a tall/narrow footprint should combine both signals.
    df["height_area_ratio"] = df["height_percentage"] / df["area_percentage"].clip(lower=1)

    # Occupants per floor.
    df["family_density"] = df["count_families"] / df["count_floors_pre_eq"].clip(lower=1)

    # Count of distinct superstructure materials reported (Section 8: 68% of buildings
    # report exactly one -- mixed-material construction may behave differently).
    df["superstructure_material_count"] = df[SUPERSTRUCTURE_COLS].sum(axis=1)

    # Count of secondary uses (sub-flags only -- excludes the has_secondary_use umbrella,
    # which is a pure OR of these and would just duplicate the same information).
    df["secondary_use_count"] = df[SECONDARY_USE_SUB_COLS].sum(axis=1)

    # foundation_type was the strongest single categorical predictor in the EDA (Section 9);
    # position split the target more modestly. Their interaction may capture combined
    # structural-vulnerability patterns neither column shows alone.
    df["foundation_position"] = df["foundation_type"] + "_" + df["position"]

    return df


# geo_level_2_id frequency map -- fit on train only. This is a row count, not target-based,
# so (unlike KFoldTargetEncoder) no out-of-fold split is needed to avoid leakage.
geo2_freq_map = train_values_clean["geo_level_2_id"].value_counts()

train_values_fe = engineer_features(train_values_clean)
test_values_fe = engineer_features(test_values_clean)

train_values_fe["geo2_freq"] = train_values_fe["geo_level_2_id"].map(geo2_freq_map).fillna(0).astype(int)
test_values_fe["geo2_freq"] = test_values_fe["geo_level_2_id"].map(geo2_freq_map).fillna(0).astype(int)

new_cols = [c for c in train_values_fe.columns if c not in train_values_clean.columns]
print("New engineered columns:", new_cols)
train_values_fe[new_cols].head()

Encoder Classes¶
Two custom BaseEstimator/TransformerMixin transformers, both designed to sit inside a
ColumnTransformer:


    

  • KFoldTargetEncoder -- out-of-fold smoothed target mean. fit_transform(X, y) (called
when the pipeline is fit on train) returns leakage-safe out-of-fold encodings via
StratifiedKFold; transform(X) (called on test) applies a mapping fit on the full training
data, falling back to the global train mean for anything unseen.
    • 

  • GeoFrequencyEncoder -- plain row-count frequency. Since it never touches the target,
ordinary fit/transform is already leakage-safe -- no out-of-fold split needed.
    • 













In [72]:






class KFoldTargetEncoder(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """
    Out-of-fold smoothed target encoding for one or more categorical
    columns, fit inside a ColumnTransformer/Pipeline.
    """

    def __init__(self, n_splits=N_SPLITS_TARGET_ENCODING,
                 smoothing=TARGET_ENCODING_SMOOTHING, random_state=RANDOM_STATE):
        self.n_splits = n_splits
        self.smoothing = smoothing
        self.random_state = random_state

    @staticmethod
    def _smoothed_means(y, groups, global_mean, smoothing):
        tmp = pd.DataFrame({"_y": np.asarray(y, dtype=float), "_grp": np.asarray(groups)})
        agg = tmp.groupby("_grp")["_y"].agg(["mean", "count"])
        return (agg["count"] * agg["mean"] + smoothing * global_mean) / (agg["count"] + smoothing)

    def fit(self, X, y):
        X = pd.DataFrame(X)
        y = pd.Series(np.asarray(y, dtype=float), index=X.index)
        self.feature_names_in_ = list(X.columns)
        self.global_mean_ = float(y.mean())
        self.full_maps_ = {
            col: self._smoothed_means(y, X[col], self.global_mean_, self.smoothing)
            for col in self.feature_names_in_
        }
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        check_is_fitted(self, "full_maps_")
        X = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=self.feature_names_in_)
        out = pd.DataFrame(index=X.index)
        for col in self.feature_names_in_:
            out[col] = X[col].map(self.full_maps_[col]).fillna(self.global_mean_)
        return out.astype(float)

    def fit_transform(self, X, y=None):
        # Overridden (rather than relying on TransformerMixin's default
        # fit(X, y).transform(X)) so TRAIN gets leakage-safe out-of-fold
        # encodings instead of each row seeing a mapping fit on itself.
        X = pd.DataFrame(X)
        y = pd.Series(np.asarray(y, dtype=float), index=X.index)
        self.feature_names_in_ = list(X.columns)
        self.global_mean_ = float(y.mean())

        oof = pd.DataFrame(index=X.index, columns=self.feature_names_in_, dtype=float)
        skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=self.n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=self.random_state)
        for train_idx, val_idx in skf.split(X, y):
            X_tr, y_tr = X.iloc[train_idx], y.iloc[train_idx]
            X_val = X.iloc[val_idx]
            for col in self.feature_names_in_:
                fold_map = self._smoothed_means(y_tr, X_tr[col], self.global_mean_, self.smoothing)
                oof.loc[X_val.index, col] = X_val[col].map(fold_map).fillna(self.global_mean_)

        self.full_maps_ = {
            col: self._smoothed_means(y, X[col], self.global_mean_, self.smoothing)
            for col in self.feature_names_in_
        }
        return oof.astype(float)

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        names = self.feature_names_in_ if input_features is None else input_features
        return np.array([c.replace("_id", "_te") for c in names])


class GeoFrequencyEncoder(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Frequency (row-count) encoding for one or more categorical columns."""

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = pd.DataFrame(X)
        self.feature_names_in_ = list(X.columns)
        self.freq_maps_ = {col: X[col].value_counts() for col in self.feature_names_in_}
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        check_is_fitted(self, "freq_maps_")
        X = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=self.feature_names_in_)
        out = pd.DataFrame(index=X.index)
        for col in self.feature_names_in_:
            out[col] = X[col].map(self.freq_maps_[col]).fillna(0)
        return out.astype(float)

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        names = self.feature_names_in_ if input_features is None else input_features
        return np.array([c.replace("_id", "_freq") for c in names])

















Geo Encoding Strategy Comparison¶
The EDA (Section 5) argued for target encoding over one-hot for the geo columns, based on
cardinality and unseen test-set categories. This checks that argument empirically instead of
taking it on faith: three full preprocessing-pipeline variants -- differing only in how
geo_level_1/2/3_id are encoded -- are each cross-validated with the same fast proxy classifier
(LogisticRegression), and whichever wins (GEO_ENCODING_STRATEGY) is what the real pipeline
below actually uses.

Full one-hot for geo_level_2_id / geo_level_3_id is deliberately excluded -- at 1,418 /
11,861 levels it would blow up the feature space and can't generalize to the unseen test-set
categories the EDA flagged there.












In [73]:






from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score


def get_geo_transformers(strategy):
    """ColumnTransformer transformer-tuples handling the 3 geo columns for a given
    strategy -- lets Stage 1 below be built generically off GEO_ENCODING_STRATEGY."""
    if strategy == "target":
        return [("geo_te", KFoldTargetEncoder(), GEO_TARGET_ENCODE_COLS)]
    if strategy == "frequency":
        return [("geo_freq", GeoFrequencyEncoder(), GEO_TARGET_ENCODE_COLS)]
    if strategy == "onehot_geo1_freq_rest":
        return [
            ("geo1_ohe", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), ["geo_level_1_id"]),
            ("geo23_freq", GeoFrequencyEncoder(), ["geo_level_2_id", "geo_level_3_id"]),
        ]
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown geo encoding strategy: {strategy!r}")


def get_geo_scale_cols(strategy):
    """Names of the geo-derived columns that need MinMax scaling in Stage 2 (one-hot
    dummies are already 0/1 and are left alone)."""
    if strategy == "target":
        return [c.replace("_id", "_te") for c in GEO_TARGET_ENCODE_COLS]
    if strategy == "frequency":
        return [c.replace("_id", "_freq") for c in GEO_TARGET_ENCODE_COLS]
    if strategy == "onehot_geo1_freq_rest":
        return [c.replace("_id", "_freq") for c in ["geo_level_2_id", "geo_level_3_id"]]
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown geo encoding strategy: {strategy!r}")


def build_geo_comparison_pipeline(strategy):
    fe = ColumnTransformer(
        transformers=get_geo_transformers(strategy) + [
            ("cont", "passthrough", CONTINUOUS_NUMERIC_COLS),
            ("ohe", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), ONE_HOT_COLS),
            ("binary", "passthrough", BINARY_COLS),
        ],
        remainder="drop",
        verbose_feature_names_out=False,
    ).set_output(transform="pandas")

    scale_cols = CONTINUOUS_NUMERIC_COLS + get_geo_scale_cols(strategy)
    scale = ColumnTransformer(
        transformers=[("minmax", MinMaxScaler(), scale_cols)],
        remainder="passthrough",
        verbose_feature_names_out=False,
    ).set_output(transform="pandas")

    return Pipeline([
        ("feature_engineering", fe),
        ("scaling", scale),
        ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE)),
    ])


geo_cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
geo_strategy_scores = {}
for strategy in ["target", "frequency", "onehot_geo1_freq_rest"]:
    pipe = build_geo_comparison_pipeline(strategy)
    scores = cross_val_score(
        pipe, train_values_fe, train_labels_clean[TARGET_COL],
        cv=geo_cv, scoring="f1_micro", n_jobs=-1,
    )
    geo_strategy_scores[strategy] = scores
    print(f"{strategy:25s}  f1_micro = {scores.mean():.4f} +/- {scores.std():.4f}")

GEO_ENCODING_STRATEGY = max(geo_strategy_scores, key=lambda s: geo_strategy_scores[s].mean())
print(f"\nSelected geo encoding strategy: {GEO_ENCODING_STRATEGY!r}")

frequency                  f1_micro = 0.5194 +/- 0.0013
onehot_geo1_freq_rest      f1_micro = 0.5932 +/- 0.0020

Preprocessing Pipeline (ColumnTransformer)¶
One-hot encoding, geo encoding (whichever strategy won above), and scaling are expressed below
as a single sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline of two ColumnTransformer stages. The pipeline is
fit_transform'd once on train (using y_train) and transform'd on test, so both sets go
through exactly the same fitted encoders/scaler -- and the whole thing is one object that can be
dropped straight into cross-validation later.














Stage 1 -- Encode¶
One ColumnTransformer fit on train_values_fe (needs y_train only if GEO_ENCODING_STRATEGY == "target", since that's the only geo option that touches the target):


    

  • geo columns: whichever strategy won the comparison above (get_geo_transformers)
    • 

  • cont: passthrough for the continuous numeric columns, including the engineered numeric
features (scaled in Stage 2)
    • 

  • ohe: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") on the 8 categorical columns plus the
engineered foundation_position and age_bucket columns
    • 

  • binary: passthrough for the superstructure / secondary-use flags plus the engineered
age_is_placeholder flag
    • 



verbose_feature_names_out=False keeps the readable original/encoded column names instead of
transformername__colname prefixes.

        ("binary", "passthrough", BINARY_COLS),
    ],
    remainder="drop",

).set_output(transform="pandas")

            verbose_feature_names_out
            
            verbose_feature_names_out: bool, str or Callable[[str, str], str], default=True

- If True, :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will prefix
  all feature names with the name of the transformer that generated that
  feature. It is equivalent to setting
  `verbose_feature_names_out="{transformer_name}__{feature_name}"`.
- If False, :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will not
  prefix any feature names and will error if feature names are not
  unique.
- If ``Callable[[str, str], str]``,
  :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will rename all the features
  using the name of the transformer. The first argument of the callable is the
  transformer name and the second argument is the feature name. The returned
  string will be the new feature name.
- If ``str``, it must be a string ready for formatting. The given string will
  be formatted using two field names: ``transformer_name`` and ``feature_name``.
  e.g. ``"{feature_name}__{transformer_name}"``. See :meth:`str.format` method
  from the standard library for more info.

.. versionadded:: 1.0

.. versionchanged:: 1.6
    `verbose_feature_names_out` can be a callable or a string to be formatted.

            remainder
            
            remainder: {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator, default='drop'

By default, only the specified columns in `transformers` are
transformed and combined in the output, and the non-specified
columns are dropped. (default of ``'drop'``).
By specifying ``remainder='passthrough'``, all remaining columns that
were not specified in `transformers`, but present in the data passed
to `fit` will be automatically passed through. This subset of columns
is concatenated with the output of the transformers. For dataframes,
extra columns not seen during `fit` will be excluded from the output
of `transform`.
By setting ``remainder`` to be an estimator, the remaining
non-specified columns will use the ``remainder`` estimator. The
estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Note that using this feature requires that the DataFrame columns
input at :term:`fit` and :term:`transform` have identical order.


'drop'

            sparse_threshold: float, default=0.3

If the output of the different transformers contains sparse matrices,
these will be stacked as a sparse matrix if the overall density is
lower than this value. Use ``sparse_threshold=0`` to always return
dense.  When the transformed output consists of all dense data, the
stacked result will be dense, and this keyword will be ignored.

            sparse_output

When ``True``, it returns a SciPy sparse matrix/array
in "Compressed Sparse Row" (CSR) format.

.. versionadded:: 1.2

False







            handle_unknown
            
            handle_unknown: {'error', 'ignore', 'infrequent_if_exist', 'warn'},                      default='error'

Specifies the way unknown categories are handled during :meth:`transform`.

- 'error' : Raise an error if an unknown category is present during transform.
- 'ignore' : When an unknown category is encountered during
  transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this feature
  will be all zeros. In the inverse transform, an unknown category
  will be denoted as None.
- 'infrequent_if_exist' : When an unknown category is encountered
  during transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this
  feature will map to the infrequent category if it exists. The
  infrequent category will be mapped to the last position in the
  encoding. During inverse transform, an unknown category will be
  mapped to the category denoted `'infrequent'` if it exists. If the
  `'infrequent'` category does not exist, then :meth:`transform` and
  :meth:`inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
  `handle_unknown='ignore'`. Infrequent categories exist based on
  `min_frequency` and `max_categories`. Read more in the
  :ref:`User Guide <encoder_infrequent_categories>`.
- 'warn' : When an unknown category is encountered during transform
  a warning is issued, and the encoding then proceeds as described for
  `handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"`.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
    `'infrequent_if_exist'` was added to automatically handle unknown
    categories and infrequent categories.

.. versionadded:: 1.6
   The option `"warn"` was added in 1.6.


'ignore'







            categories
            
            categories: 'auto' or a list of array-like, default='auto'

Categories (unique values) per feature:

- 'auto' : Determine categories automatically from the training data.
- list : ``categories[i]`` holds the categories expected in the ith
  column. The passed categories should not mix strings and numeric
  values within a single feature, and should be sorted in case of
  numeric values.

The used categories can be found in the ``categories_`` attribute.

.. versionadded:: 0.20


'auto'







            drop
            
            drop: {'first', 'if_binary'} or an array-like of shape (n_features,),             default=None

Specifies a methodology to use to drop one of the categories per
feature. This is useful in situations where perfectly collinear
features cause problems, such as when feeding the resulting data
into an unregularized linear regression model.

However, dropping one category breaks the symmetry of the original
representation and can therefore induce a bias in downstream models,
for instance for penalized linear classification or regression models.

- None : retain all features (the default).
- 'first' : drop the first category in each feature. If only one
  category is present, the feature will be dropped entirely.
- 'if_binary' : drop the first category in each feature with two
  categories. Features with 1 or more than 2 categories are
  left intact.
- array : ``drop[i]`` is the category in feature ``X[:, i]`` that
  should be dropped.

When `max_categories` or `min_frequency` is configured to group
infrequent categories, the dropping behavior is handled after the
grouping.

.. versionadded:: 0.21
   The parameter `drop` was added in 0.21.

.. versionchanged:: 0.23
   The option `drop='if_binary'` was added in 0.23.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
    Support for dropping infrequent categories.


None







            dtype
            
            dtype: number type, default=np.float64

Desired dtype of output.


<class 'numpy.float64'>







            min_frequency
            
            min_frequency: int or float, default=None

Specifies the minimum frequency below which a category will be
considered infrequent.

- If `int`, categories with a smaller cardinality will be considered
  infrequent.

- If `float`, categories with a smaller cardinality than
  `min_frequency * n_samples`  will be considered infrequent.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
    Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <encoder_infrequent_categories>`.


None







            max_categories
            
            max_categories: int, default=None

Specifies an upper limit to the number of output features for each input
feature when considering infrequent categories. If there are infrequent
categories, `max_categories` includes the category representing the
infrequent categories along with the frequent categories. If `None`,
there is no limit to the number of output features.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
    Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <encoder_infrequent_categories>`.


None







            feature_name_combiner
            
            feature_name_combiner: "concat" or callable, default="concat"

Callable with signature `def callable(input_feature, category)` that returns a
string. This is used to create feature names to be returned by
:meth:`get_feature_names_out`.

`"concat"` concatenates encoded feature name and category with
`feature + "_" + str(category)`.E.g. feature X with values 1, 6, 7 create

Stage 2 -- Scale¶
A second ColumnTransformer, chained after Stage 1 by column name, applies MinMaxScaler to
the continuous numeric + geo-encoded columns and passes every other column (one-hot + binary
flags, already 0/1) straight through unscaled. The two stages are combined into a single
Pipeline so fit_transform/transform run both stages in sequence.

            sparse_output
            
            sparse_output: bool, default=True

When ``True``, it returns a SciPy sparse matrix/array
in "Compressed Sparse Row" (CSR) format.

.. versionadded:: 1.2
   `sparse` was renamed to `sparse_output`


False







            handle_unknown
            
            handle_unknown: {'error', 'ignore', 'infrequent_if_exist', 'warn'},                      default='error'

Specifies the way unknown categories are handled during :meth:`transform`.

- 'error' : Raise an error if an unknown category is present during transform.
- 'ignore' : When an unknown category is encountered during
  transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this feature
  will be all zeros. In the inverse transform, an unknown category
  will be denoted as None.
- 'infrequent_if_exist' : When an unknown category is encountered
  during transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this
  feature will map to the infrequent category if it exists. The
  infrequent category will be mapped to the last position in the
  encoding. During inverse transform, an unknown category will be
  mapped to the category denoted `'infrequent'` if it exists. If the
  `'infrequent'` category does not exist, then :meth:`transform` and
  :meth:`inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
  `handle_unknown='ignore'`. Infrequent categories exist based on
  `min_frequency` and `max_categories`. Read more in the
  :ref:`User Guide <encoder_infrequent_categories>`.
- 'warn' : When an unknown category is encountered during transform
  a warning is issued, and the encoding then proceeds as described for
  `handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"`.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
    `'infrequent_if_exist'` was added to automatically handle unknown
    categories and infrequent categories.

.. versionadded:: 1.6
   The option `"warn"` was added in 1.6.


'ignore'







            categories
            
            categories: 'auto' or a list of array-like, default='auto'

Categories (unique values) per feature:

- 'auto' : Determine categories automatically from the training data.
- list : ``categories[i]`` holds the categories expected in the ith
  column. The passed categories should not mix strings and numeric
  values within a single feature, and should be sorted in case of
  numeric values.

The used categories can be found in the ``categories_`` attribute.

.. versionadded:: 0.20


'auto'







            drop
            
            drop: {'first', 'if_binary'} or an array-like of shape (n_features,),             default=None

Specifies a methodology to use to drop one of the categories per
feature. This is useful in situations where perfectly collinear
features cause problems, such as when feeding the resulting data
into an unregularized linear regression model.

However, dropping one category breaks the symmetry of the original
representation and can therefore induce a bias in downstream models,
for instance for penalized linear classification or regression models.

- None : retain all features (the default).
- 'first' : drop the first category in each feature. If only one
  category is present, the feature will be dropped entirely.
- 'if_binary' : drop the first category in each feature with two
  categories. Features with 1 or more than 2 categories are
  left intact.
- array : ``drop[i]`` is the category in feature ``X[:, i]`` that
  should be dropped.

When `max_categories` or `min_frequency` is configured to group
infrequent categories, the dropping behavior is handled after the
grouping.

.. versionadded:: 0.21
   The parameter `drop` was added in 0.21.

.. versionchanged:: 0.23
   The option `drop='if_binary'` was added in 0.23.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
    Support for dropping infrequent categories.


None







            dtype
            
            dtype: number type, default=np.float64

Desired dtype of output.


<class 'numpy.float64'>







            min_frequency
            
            min_frequency: int or float, default=None

Specifies the minimum frequency below which a category will be
considered infrequent.

- If `int`, categories with a smaller cardinality will be considered
  infrequent.

- If `float`, categories with a smaller cardinality than
  `min_frequency * n_samples`  will be considered infrequent.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
    Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <encoder_infrequent_categories>`.


None







            max_categories
            
            max_categories: int, default=None

Specifies an upper limit to the number of output features for each input
feature when considering infrequent categories. If there are infrequent
categories, `max_categories` includes the category representing the
infrequent categories along with the frequent categories. If `None`,
there is no limit to the number of output features.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
    Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <encoder_infrequent_categories>`.


None







            feature_name_combiner
            
            feature_name_combiner: "concat" or callable, default="concat"

Callable with signature `def callable(input_feature, category)` that returns a
string. This is used to create feature names to be returned by
:meth:`get_feature_names_out`.

`"concat"` concatenates encoded feature name and category with
`feature + "_" + str(category)`.E.g. feature X with values 1, 6, 7 create
feature names `X_1, X_6, X_7`.

.. versionadded:: 1.3


'concat'

Parameters








            transformers
            
            transformers: list of tuples

List of (name, transformer, columns) tuples specifying the
transformer objects to be applied to subsets of the data.

name : str
    Like in Pipeline and FeatureUnion, this allows the transformer and
    its parameters to be set using ``set_params`` and searched in grid
    search.
transformer : {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator
    Estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
    Special-cased strings 'drop' and 'passthrough' are accepted as
    well, to indicate to drop the columns or to pass them through
    untransformed, respectively.
columns :  str, array-like of str, int, array-like of int,                 array-like of bool, slice or callable
    Indexes the data on its second axis. Integers are interpreted as
    positional columns, while strings can reference DataFrame columns
    by name.  A scalar string or int should be used where
    ``transformer`` expects X to be a 1d array-like (vector),
    otherwise a 2d array will be passed to the transformer.
    A callable is passed the input data `X` and can return any of the
    above. To select multiple columns by name or dtype, you can use
    :obj:`make_column_selector`.


[('minmax', ...)]







            remainder
            
            remainder: {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator, default='drop'

By default, only the specified columns in `transformers` are
transformed and combined in the output, and the non-specified
columns are dropped. (default of ``'drop'``).
By specifying ``remainder='passthrough'``, all remaining columns that
were not specified in `transformers`, but present in the data passed
to `fit` will be automatically passed through. This subset of columns
is concatenated with the output of the transformers. For dataframes,
extra columns not seen during `fit` will be excluded from the output
of `transform`.
By setting ``remainder`` to be an estimator, the remaining
non-specified columns will use the ``remainder`` estimator. The
estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Note that using this feature requires that the DataFrame columns
input at :term:`fit` and :term:`transform` have identical order.


'passthrough'







            verbose_feature_names_out
            
            verbose_feature_names_out: bool, str or Callable[[str, str], str], default=True

- If True, :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will prefix
  all feature names with the name of the transformer that generated that
  feature. It is equivalent to setting
  `verbose_feature_names_out="{transformer_name}__{feature_name}"`.
- If False, :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will not
  prefix any feature names and will error if feature names are not
  unique.
- If ``Callable[[str, str], str]``,
  :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will rename all the features
  using the name of the transformer. The first argument of the callable is the
  transformer name and the second argument is the feature name. The returned
  string will be the new feature name.
- If ``str``, it must be a string ready for formatting. The given string will
  be formatted using two field names: ``transformer_name`` and ``feature_name``.
  e.g. ``"{feature_name}__{transformer_name}"``. See :meth:`str.format` method
  from the standard library for more info.

            clip
            
            clip: bool, default=False

Set to True to clip transformed values of held-out data to
provided `feature_range`.
Since this parameter will clip values, `inverse_transform` may not
be able to restore the original data.

.. note::
    Setting `clip=True` does not prevent feature drift (a distribution
    shift between training and test data). The transformed values are clipped
    to the `feature_range`, which helps avoid unintended behavior in models
    sensitive to out-of-range inputs (e.g. linear models). Use with care,
    as clipping can distort the distribution of test data.

Fit on Train, Transform Test¶
Fit on train_values_fe + y_train only. Test (test_values_fe) only ever sees .transform --
the target-encoding fallback (global train mean) and OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")
cover any category unseen during fit.

Feature Selection¶
train_final now has more columns than the model strictly needs after one-hot encoding, geo
encoding, and the engineered features above -- including at least one pair known to be
redundant by construction (age_bucket_unknown and age_is_placeholder encode the same 995
sentinel). Two complementary checks trim it down:


    

  1. Redundancy check -- flag any pair of numeric/encoded columns with |Pearson r| > 0.85
(stricter than the 0.77 max correlation already logged in the EDA appendix), since
near-duplicate columns add noise to linear/distance-based methods and dilute importance
estimates without adding signal.
    2. 

  2. Embedded importance -- fit a quick RandomForestClassifier on the full feature set and
keep only the columns at or above the median importance
(SelectFromModel(threshold="median")), cross-checked against a mutual-information ranking
so the selection isn't tied to one estimator's quirks.
    3. 



The result, SELECTED_FEATURES, is the default feature set used for modeling below;
ALL_FEATURES (the full engineered set) is kept alongside it so the choice can be compared
directly.














Redundancy Check¶












In [80]:






numeric_like_cols = [
    c for c in train_final.columns
    if c not in (ID_COL, TARGET_COL) and train_final[c].nunique() > 2
]

corr_matrix = train_final[numeric_like_cols].corr().abs()
upper = corr_matrix.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr_matrix.shape), k=1).astype(bool))

redundant_pairs = [
    (row, col, upper.loc[row, col])
    for col in upper.columns
    for row in upper.index
    if pd.notna(upper.loc[row, col]) and upper.loc[row, col] > 0.85
]

print(f"Pairs with |corr| > 0.85: {len(redundant_pairs)}")
for a, b, v in sorted(redundant_pairs, key=lambda t: -t[2]):
    print(f"  {a:35s} <-> {b:35s}  r = {v:.3f}")



















Pairs with |corr| > 0.85: 2
  age                                 <-> age_x_floors                         r = 0.932
  geo_level_2_te                      <-> geo_level_3_te                       r = 0.887



















Embedded Importance (Random Forest + SelectFromModel)¶












In [81]:






from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

    n_estimators=300, max_depth=None, class_weight="balanced_subsample",
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1,
)

Modeling¶
Following the roadmap (steps 20-25 above): a naive baseline, a cross-validated comparison of
four candidate model families, hyperparameter tuning of the three tree ensembles, a held-out
validation check, and a final refit used to produce the competition submission. All comparisons
and tuning use f1_micro, the competition's actual metric (performance_metric.md), not
accuracy.












In [83]:






from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score, RandomizedSearchCV
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, classification_report, ConfusionMatrixDisplay
from scipy.stats import randint, uniform
from xgboost import XGBClassifier
from lightgbm import LGBMClassifier

















Feature Set & Train/Validation Split¶
FEATURE_SET defaults to SELECTED_FEATURES from the Feature Selection section above -- set it
to ALL_FEATURES to compare. A stratified 85/15 split carves out X_val/y_val as a final
check (Step 24) that is never touched during cross-validation or tuning; the CV folds below
(cv) are drawn only from X_tr/y_tr.












In [84]:






FEATURE_SET = SELECTED_FEATURES  # swap to ALL_FEATURES to compare

X = train_final[FEATURE_SET]
y = train_final[TARGET_COL]
X_test_final = test_final[FEATURE_SET]

X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.15, stratify=y, random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

print(f"X_tr : {X_tr.shape}   X_val: {X_val.shape}   X_test_final: {X_test_final.shape}")



















X_tr : (221510, 50)   X_val: (39091, 50)   X_test_final: (86868, 50)



















Step 20 -- Naive Baseline¶












In [85]:






baseline = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent", random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
baseline.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
baseline_f1 = f1_score(y_val, baseline.predict(X_val), average="micro")
print(f"Naive baseline (always predict the majority class) -- f1_micro: {baseline_f1:.4f}")



















Naive baseline (always predict the majority class) -- f1_micro: 0.5689



















Step 21 -- Candidate Model Comparison (Cross-Validation)¶
Four model families spanning the spectrum the EDA pointed toward: a linear baseline
(LogisticRegression), then three tree ensembles (RandomForestClassifier, XGBClassifier,
LGBMClassifier) that can capture the non-linear/interaction-driven signal noted in Section 9.
XGBoost's sklearn wrapper requires 0-indexed class labels for multi:softprob (damage_grade - 1, shifted back by +1 on prediction); LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier, and
LGBMClassifier all handle the raw 1/2/3 labels natively via their own internal label
encoding.












In [86]:






candidates = {
    "logistic_regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "random_forest": RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=300, class_weight="balanced_subsample", random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1
    ),
    "xgboost": XGBClassifier(
        objective="multi:softprob", num_class=3, eval_metric="mlogloss",
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1
    ),
    "lightgbm": LGBMClassifier(
        class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1, verbose=-1
    ),
}

cv_results = {}
for name, model in candidates.items():
    y_fit = (y_tr - 1) if name == "xgboost" else y_tr
    scores = cross_val_score(model, X_tr, y_fit, cv=cv, scoring="f1_micro", n_jobs=-1)
    cv_results[name] = scores
    print(f"{name:20s}  f1_micro = {scores.mean():.4f} +/- {scores.std():.4f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.5))
names = list(cv_results.keys())
means = [cv_results[n].mean() for n in names]
stds = [cv_results[n].std() for n in names]
bar_colors = [CAT["blue"], CAT["aqua"], CAT["orange"], CAT["violet"]]
ax.bar(names, means, yerr=stds, capsize=4, color=bar_colors)
ax.axhline(baseline_f1, color=INK_MUTED, linestyle="--", linewidth=1, label=f"naive baseline ({baseline_f1:.3f})")
ax.set_ylabel("f1_micro (5-fold CV)")
ax.set_title("Candidate Model Comparison", color=INK_PRIMARY, fontsize=12, loc="left", pad=12)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
style_ax(ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(OUT / "model_comparison_cv.png", dpi=160)
plt.show()



















logistic_regression   f1_micro = 0.6763 +/- 0.0017
random_forest         f1_micro = 0.7392 +/- 0.0019
xgboost               f1_micro = 0.7428 +/- 0.0031
lightgbm              f1_micro = 0.6870 +/- 0.0018






























Step 22 -- Hyperparameter Tuning: Random Forest¶
RandomizedSearchCV (25 draws, 3-fold CV -- cheaper than the 5-fold comparison above given
~220K training rows) over the parameters that matter most for a RandomForestClassifier:
ensemble size, tree depth/leaf constraints, and the fraction of features considered at each
split. Reduce n_iter if this runs too slowly on your machine.












In [ ]:






rf_param_dist = {
    "n_estimators": randint(200, 600),
    "max_depth": [None] + list(range(8, 41, 4)),
    "min_samples_split": randint(2, 20),
    "min_samples_leaf": randint(1, 10),
    "max_features": ["sqrt", "log2", 0.3, 0.5],
}

rf_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    RandomForestClassifier(class_weight="balanced_subsample", random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1),
    param_distributions=rf_param_dist,
    n_iter=25,
    cv=StratifiedKFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    scoring="f1_micro",
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=1,
)
rf_search.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print("Best RF params:", rf_search.best_params_)
print(f"Best RF CV f1_micro: {rf_search.best_score_:.4f}")



















Fitting 3 folds for each of 25 candidates, totalling 75 fits



















Step 22 -- Hyperparameter Tuning: XGBoost¶
Same RandomizedSearchCV setup, over XGBoost's core boosting parameters (tree count/depth,
learning rate, subsampling, and the two regularization knobs -- min_child_weight, gamma).
Labels are shifted to 0-indexed for XGBoost, as in the comparison above.












In [ ]:






xgb_param_dist = {
    "n_estimators": randint(200, 600),
    "max_depth": randint(3, 12),
    "learning_rate": uniform(0.01, 0.29),
    "subsample": uniform(0.6, 0.4),
    "colsample_bytree": uniform(0.6, 0.4),
    "min_child_weight": randint(1, 10),
    "gamma": uniform(0, 0.5),
}

xgb_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    XGBClassifier(objective="multi:softprob", num_class=3, eval_metric="mlogloss",
                  random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1),
    param_distributions=xgb_param_dist,
    n_iter=25,
    cv=StratifiedKFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    scoring="f1_micro",
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=1,
)
xgb_search.fit(X_tr, y_tr - 1)

print("Best XGB params:", xgb_search.best_params_)
print(f"Best XGB CV f1_micro: {xgb_search.best_score_:.4f}")

















Step 22 -- Hyperparameter Tuning: LightGBM¶
Same RandomizedSearchCV setup again, over LightGBM's core boosting parameters (tree
count/depth, leaf count, learning rate, subsampling, and L1/L2 regularization). Unlike XGBoost,
LGBMClassifier handles the raw 1/2/3 labels directly -- no shifting needed.












In [ ]:






lgbm_param_dist = {
    "n_estimators": randint(200, 600),
    "num_leaves": randint(15, 127),
    "max_depth": [-1] + list(range(3, 13)),
    "learning_rate": uniform(0.01, 0.29),
    "subsample": uniform(0.6, 0.4),
    "colsample_bytree": uniform(0.6, 0.4),
    "min_child_samples": randint(5, 50),
    "reg_alpha": uniform(0, 1),
    "reg_lambda": uniform(0, 1),
}

lgbm_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    LGBMClassifier(class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1, verbose=-1),
    param_distributions=lgbm_param_dist,
    n_iter=25,
    cv=StratifiedKFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    scoring="f1_micro",
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=1,
)
lgbm_search.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print("Best LightGBM params:", lgbm_search.best_params_)
print(f"Best LightGBM CV f1_micro: {lgbm_search.best_score_:.4f}")

















Step 23-24 -- Pick the Best Candidate & Evaluate on the Held-out Split¶
Whichever tuned search scored highest on CV is checked once against X_val/y_val -- the split
neither cross-validation nor tuning ever saw.












In [ ]:






tuned_searches = {
    "random_forest": (rf_search, 0),
    "xgboost": (xgb_search, 1),
    "lightgbm": (lgbm_search, 0),
}
best_name, (best_search, label_offset) = max(tuned_searches.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1][0].best_score_)

best_model = best_search.best_estimator_
print(f"Selected model: {best_name}  (tuned CV f1_micro = {best_search.best_score_:.4f})")
for name, (search, _) in tuned_searches.items():
    print(f"  {name:15s} best CV f1_micro = {search.best_score_:.4f}")

y_val_pred = best_model.predict(X_val) + label_offset
val_f1 = f1_score(y_val, y_val_pred, average="micro")
print(f"\nHeld-out validation f1_micro: {val_f1:.4f}")
print(classification_report(y_val, y_val_pred))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(y_val, y_val_pred, ax=ax, cmap="Blues", colorbar=False)
ax.set_title(f"Held-out Validation Confusion Matrix ({best_name})", fontsize=11, loc="left")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(OUT / "final_model_confusion_matrix.png", dpi=160)
plt.show()

















Step 23 -- Refit on the Full Cleaned Training Set¶
The held-out check above used X_tr only. For the actual submission, the same tuned
hyperparameters (cloned from best_search.best_estimator_) are refit on all of
train_final (X_tr + X_val combined) so the final model sees every available labeled row.












In [ ]:






final_model = clone(best_search.best_estimator_)
if best_name == "xgboost":
    final_model.fit(X, y - 1)
else:
    final_model.fit(X, y)

print(f"Final {best_name} refit on the full training set: {X.shape[0]:,} rows.")

















Step 25 -- Predict on Test & Build the Submission¶
Predictions are written as building_id, damage_grade (integer, per submission_format.md),
and the predicted-class distribution is sanity-checked against the training distribution
(Section 4: ~9.6% / 56.9% / 33.5% for grades 1/2/3) -- a wildly different split on test would
flag a bug.












In [ ]:






test_pred = final_model.predict(X_test_final) + label_offset

submission = test_final[[ID_COL]].copy()
submission[TARGET_COL] = test_pred.astype(int)

print("Predicted damage_grade distribution (test):")
print(submission[TARGET_COL].value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index().round(4))
print("\nTrain damage_grade distribution (reference):")
print(y.value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index().round(4))

submission_path = OUTPUT_DIR / "submission.csv"
submission.to_csv(submission_path, index=False)
print(f"\nSaved: {submission_path}  ({len(submission):,} rows)")
assert len(submission) == 86868, "submission row count does not match test_values"

















Final Model Feature Importance¶












In [ ]:






final_importances = pd.Series(final_model.feature_importances_, index=FEATURE_SET).sort_values()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, max(4, 0.3 * len(FEATURE_SET))))
ax.barh(final_importances.index, final_importances.values, color=CAT["blue"], height=0.65)
ax.set_xlabel("Feature importance")
ax.set_title(f"Final Model ({best_name}) Feature Importance", color=INK_PRIMARY, fontsize=12, loc="left", pad=12)
style_ax(ax, hide_spines=("top", "right", "left"))
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(OUT / "final_model_feature_importance.png", dpi=160)
plt.show()

















Model Explainability (SHAP)¶
shap.TreeExplainer works natively on all three tuned tree ensembles
(RandomForestClassifier, XGBClassifier, LGBMClassifier), so it applies directly to
whichever final_model was selected above -- no special-casing needed. SHAP values are computed
on a random sample of the held-out validation set (X_val): large enough to be representative,
small enough to compute quickly. They're read per class: a beeswarm plot for damage_grade == 3 (severe damage / near-total destruction) answers the question this analysis has been
building toward -- which building characteristics push a prediction toward the worst damage
outcome, and in which direction.












In [ ]:






import shap

SHAP_SAMPLE_SIZE = min(2000, len(X_val))
X_shap = X_val.sample(SHAP_SAMPLE_SIZE, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(final_model)
raw_shap_values = explainer.shap_values(X_shap)

# final_model.classes_ holds the model's *internal* labels -- 0/1/2 for XGBoost (labels were
# shifted at fit time, see Step 23), 1/2/3 for RandomForest/LightGBM. label_offset (from Step
# 23-24) maps these back to the real damage_grade values (1/2/3) used everywhere else, so
# shap_by_class can always be indexed by the real grade regardless of which model won.
if isinstance(raw_shap_values, list):
    per_class_values = {cls: raw_shap_values[i] for i, cls in enumerate(final_model.classes_)}
elif raw_shap_values.ndim == 3:
    per_class_values = {cls: raw_shap_values[:, :, i] for i, cls in enumerate(final_model.classes_)}
else:
    per_class_values = {final_model.classes_[0]: raw_shap_values}

shap_by_class = {int(cls) + label_offset: vals for cls, vals in per_class_values.items()}

print(f"SHAP values computed for {SHAP_SAMPLE_SIZE:,} validation rows, "
      f"damage_grade classes: {sorted(shap_by_class)}.")

















Beeswarm: What Drives Each Damage-Grade Prediction (Grades 1-3)¶












In [ ]:






grade_labels = {1: "Low Damage", 2: "Medium Damage", 3: "Severe Damage (Near-Total Destruction)"}

for grade in sorted(shap_by_class):
    shap.summary_plot(shap_by_class[grade], X_shap, show=False, max_display=15)
    fig = plt.gcf()
    fig.set_size_inches(9, 7)
    plt.title(f"SHAP -- Feature Impact on Predicting {grade_labels[grade]} (grade {grade})", loc="left", fontsize=12)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(OUT / f"shap_summary_grade{grade}.png", dpi=160)
    plt.show()

















Overall Ranking: Strongest Predictors Across All Grades¶












In [ ]:






mean_abs_shap = pd.DataFrame(
    {f"grade_{cls}": np.abs(vals).mean(axis=0) for cls, vals in shap_by_class.items()},
    index=X_shap.columns,
)
mean_abs_shap["overall"] = mean_abs_shap.mean(axis=1)
top_shap = mean_abs_shap.sort_values("overall", ascending=False).head(15)

print("Top 15 features by mean |SHAP value| (averaged across all classes):")
print(top_shap.round(4))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 7))
plot_shap = top_shap["overall"].sort_values(ascending=True)
ax.barh(plot_shap.index, plot_shap.values, color=CAT["violet"], height=0.65)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean |SHAP value| (avg across classes)")
ax.set_title(f"Strongest Predictors of damage_grade -- SHAP ({best_name})", color=INK_PRIMARY, fontsize=12, loc="left", pad=12)
style_ax(ax, hide_spines=("top", "right", "left"))
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(OUT / "shap_overall_importance.png", dpi=160)
plt.show()

















Interpretation: The beeswarm plot shows, feature-by-feature, which values push an
individual prediction toward severe damage -- not just how important a feature is on average,
but whether high values of it (red) cluster on the positive-SHAP side or the negative one.
Combined with the ranked bar chart above, this closes the loop back to the EDA's Section 9
finding that location (geo_level_*) and superstructure/foundation material dominate the
signal -- SHAP confirms whether that holds for the specific tuned model driving the submission,
rather than the raw association strength computed before any modeling was done.
